scenes.narration: The unconscious does not argue with The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man; it simply acts first. The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man (1912/1927) by James Weldon Johnson is the fictional account of a young biracial man, referred to only as the "Ex-Colored Man", living in post-Reconstruction era America in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. He lives through a variety of experiences, including witnessing a lynching, that convince him to "pass" as white to secure his safety and advancement, but he feels as if he has given up his dream of "glorifying" the black race by composing ragtime music.

The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man feels chosen. The evidence says it was installed. Johnson originally published The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man anonymously in 1912, via the small Boston publisher Sherman, French, & Company. He decided to publish it anonymously because he was uncertain how the potentially controversial book would affect his diplomatic career.

The bleak reading of The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man is also the most testable one. He wrote openly about issues of race and discrimination that were not common then in literature. Knopf, an influential firm that published many Harlem Renaissance writers, and Johnson was credited as the author.

Modern psychology keeps rediscovering what the pessimists said first about The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man. It is drawn from the lives of people Johnson knew and from events in his life. The narrator also chooses to withhold the name of the small Georgia town where his narrative begins, as there are still living residents of the town who might be able to connect him to the narrative.

The self that experiences The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man is a committee, not a king. Throughout the novel, the adult narrator from the frame interjects into the text to offer reflective commentary into the events of the narrative. Born shortly after the Civil War in a small Georgia town, the narrator's African-American mother protected him as a child and teenager.

Reproduction explains more of The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man than any philosophy dares to admit. The narrator's father, a wealthy white member of the Southern aristocracy, is absent throughout the narrator's childhood but, nevertheless, continues to provide financial support for the narrator and his mother. Because of that financial support, she had the means to raise her son in an environment more middle-class than many black people could enjoy at the time.

Once you see The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man as an adaptation, the mystery mostly evaporates. The narrator describes learning to love music at a young age as well as attending an integrated school. It is while attending this school that the narrator first realizes he is African-American and thus subject to ridicule and mistreatment for his racial heritage.

The story The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man tells about itself is the last thing to be trusted. This "discovery" occurs when he is publicly corrected by his teacher and the headmaster when he stands when "the white scholars" (schoolchildren) are asked to stand. While in school, the narrator also grows to admire and befriends "Shiny," an unmistakably African-American boy, who is described as one of the brightest and best-spoken children in the class.

Meaning is not found in The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man — it is manufactured for it. He adapted very well to life with lower-class black people and was able to move easily among the classes of black society. During this carefree period, he taught music and attended church, where he came in contact with upper-class black people.

The cold light on The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man leaves the facts intact and only the comfort removed. Living in an all black community, he discovers and describes three classes of black people: the desperate, the domestics, and the independent workmen or professionals. The Ex-Colored Man believed the desperate class consists of lower-class black people who loathe the whites.

The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man did not evolve to be understood — only to be survived. The domestic worker class comprises black people who work as servants to whites. And the artisans, skilled workers, and black professionals class included black people who had little interaction with the whites.

The honest version of The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man starts by giving up the comforting part. Many white readers, who viewed all black people as a stereotype of a single class, were unfamiliar with class distinctions described among black people. While playing ragtime at a late night hotspot in New York, the Ex-Colored Man caught the attention of a wealthy white gentleman.

Strip The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. The gentleman's liking for ragtime develops as liking for the Ex-Colored Man himself. The white gentleman hired him to play ragtime piano for guests at parties.

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man shows exactly where that breaks. Soon the Ex-Colored Man spent most of his time working for the white gentleman, who paid him to play ragtime music for hours at a time. He would play until the white gentleman would say "that will do." The Ex-Colored man would tire after the long hours but would continue playing as he saw the joy and serenity he brought the white gentleman.

What looks like free choice in The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man is older than choice itself. The white gentleman frequently "loaned" the Ex-Colored Man out to other people to play at their parties. The gentleman was not "loaning" him out as a piece of property, but simply giving the narrator a broader palette to display his talents.

Nobody designed the part of The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man you experience — it was inherited. The Ex-Colored man saw how the rich lived; he was thrilled to live in this lifestyle. The Rich White Gentleman influenced the Ex-Colored Man more than anyone else he met.

Every serious account of The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. In his relationship toward the Rich White Man he was aware of aspects of the slave/master, but saw there was also one of friendship. While he was with the white gentleman, the Ex-Colored Man decided he would use his skills to aid in abolitionism.

Nihilism is not the conclusion of The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man — it is the floor you stand on while examining it. Even though life was pleasant, it was void of substance; using his music to aid poor African Americans he felt would be a better use of his talents. The Ex-Colored Man continued to show devotion to the white gentleman, as the white gentleman treated him with kindness, which eventually led to the forming a friendship while in Paris.

The selfish-gene reading of The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man makes it less romantic and far more precise. The Ex-Colored Man's devotion to the white gentleman expresses the relationship that some slaves had with their masters (slaves who showed devotion to the slave-owner). Johnson suggests that, although the Ex-Colored Man had "freedom," he was still suffering from the effects of slavery.

Freud is not dead; he is simply no longer allowed to be the whole answer. After playing for the white gentleman while touring Europe, the Ex-Colored Man decided to leave him and return to the South to study Negro spirituals. He planned to use his knowledge of classical and ragtime music to create a new Black American musical genre.

The feeling that The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man means something is a chemical event with an evolutionary address. He wanted to "bring glory and honor to the Negro race," to return to his heritage, and proud and self-righteous race. The narrator's time in Paris, however, is cut short when he goes to see a performance of Faust, during which he sits next to a beautiful young woman for whom he initially expresses great admiration.

Nothing in The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man was built for you — it was built for reproduction. This event leaves a deep impression upon the narrator and causes him to decide to leave the company of his patron (the Rich White Gentleman) to return to the United States on his mission of advancing African-American musical forms. Just as the Ex-Colored Man began to work on his music in the South, he witnessed the lynching of a black man.

The psychology underneath The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man is simpler and older than the story on top. The Ex-Colored Man narrates in detail what he saw, "He squirmed, he withered, strained at his chains, then gave out cries and groans that I shall always hear."  The narrator is horrified by the extent of this violent racism played out in the town square. He gives up his dream of making music to glorify his race and thinks he does not want to be "identified with people that could with impunity be treated worse than animals," or with people who could treat other humans that way.

Behind The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man sits an animal brain negotiating with a story it tells itself. The narrator eventually begins a courtship with a white woman, causing an internal dilemma as to whether or not to reveal his African-American heritage, and he asks her to marry him. After the two have a chance meeting with Shiny, in which the narrator is "surprised at the amount of interest a refined black man could arouse," the narrator decides to reveal his secret to her.

The nihilist does not deny The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man — he only refuses to flatter it. At first shocked, she flees, and the narrator resolves to give her sufficient space to let her make up her mind. Eventually, she returns to him, having absorbed his revelation and chosen to accept him.

What culture calls destiny in The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man is usually just selection pressure wearing a suit. They are eventually married and have two children, and the narrator lives out his life as a successful yet mediocre businessman. His wife dies during the birth of their second child, leaving the narrator alone to raise their two children.

The genes do not care about The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man; they care about copies. "Passing" could be interpreted as a decision to avoid the black race. He states that he "regrets holding himself back." He may have been implying that if he had, he embraced the Negro community and let the community embrace him, that he could have made a difference.

Take away the meaning and The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man still functions — that is the disturbing part. The Ex-Colored Man was one of the few people who was not held back by being black. Because of his fear of being a Negro, he threw away his talent as a musician to "become" a white man.

The unconscious does not argue with The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man; it simply acts first. This is one portrayal of the social strains due to racial discrimination; he felt that society forced him to choose between his love of African-American music and the safety and convenience of being white with the majority. The white gentleman fully accepted the Ex-Colored Man for who he was, but he feared that others would not.

The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man feels chosen. The evidence says it was installed. He decided to protect his mixed-race children by having them grow up "white." He wanted to give them every advantage he could. The narrator in some ways reflects the trope of the tragic mulatto, however, rather than suffering a catastrophic downfall; as a result, the narrator's tragedy is much more subversive.

The bleak reading of The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man is also the most testable one. The "Ex-colored Man" is compelled by fear, not only for himself but for his children's sake (so they can grow up "white"), to exist in degraded mediocrity, despite his apparent potential and lofty goals of advancing the African-American race. In this way, his boyhood friend, "Shiny," and his symbolic name, act as a foil for the narrator.

Modern psychology keeps rediscovering what the pessimists said first about The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man. The narrator has admired since childhood, his inability to "pass" forces him to accomplish, rather than merely aspire as the narrator does. At the end of the novel, Shiny has risen to refinement and prestige while embracing his racial heritage and contributing to the community, while the narrator is relegated to mediocrity and obscurity, unable to risk revealing his racial background.

The self that experiences The Autobiography of an Ex-Colored Man is a committee, not a king.
